Baby & Child

9 Month Old Milestones: Skills to Expect at 9 Months

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

At 9 months, most babies sit without support, respond to their name, string babbling sounds together like mamamama, look for objects that drop out of sight, and rake food toward themselves with their fingers. Stranger shyness, peekaboo giggles, and protest when you leave the room are also right on schedule. This guide walks through each area, plus the nine month checkup, so you know what to expect and what is worth a call to your pediatrician.

Social skills: your name, strangers, and peekaboo

Around nine months, most babies look when you call their name, even from across the room. Many also become noticeably shy, clingy, or fearful around people they do not know well, including relatives they were happy with a month ago. That shift can feel like a step backward, but it is actually a sign of progress: your baby now clearly knows the difference between familiar people and strangers. You may also notice a protest when you leave the room. That reaction has a name, separation anxiety, and it is a normal part of nine month development rather than a habit you created or a problem you need to fix.

Peekaboo usually becomes a favorite around this age. Most babies smile or laugh at peekaboo by nine months because they are starting to understand that a hidden face still exists and will come back. Every round of the game rehearses that lesson, which is one reason it never seems to get old. You can build on it with simple variations: hide a toy under a cloth and let your baby pull it off, or duck behind a door frame and pop out. Keep the pace slow and let your baby take a turn hiding too. These small games are real developmental work dressed up as play, and they cost nothing.

Babbling, gestures, and new thinking skills

Listen for long strings of repeated sounds: mamamama, babababa, dadadada. At nine months these are usually babble rather than true words, even when they sound convincing, and that is exactly on track. Your baby is practicing the building blocks of speech and learning that sounds get a response. Gestures grow alongside the babble. Many babies now lift their arms to be picked up, a small movement that is really a first conversation: I want something, and I can tell you. Answer both. When your baby babbles, pause, respond, and wait for a reply. This back-and-forth exchange teaches the rhythm of conversation long before real words arrive.

Thinking skills take a visible jump around now. Drop a spoon off the high chair tray and your baby will look down to find it, which shows they understand objects still exist out of sight. Expect this game on repeat, because the finding is the fun part. Most nine month olds also bang two things together, shake, and mouth objects to learn what they do. Offer safe household items with different textures and sounds: a wooden spoon and a pot lid work as well as any toy. Narrate what happens in plain words. You are watching cause and effect, memory, and problem solving develop in real time.

Movement at nine months, and a word about crawling

By nine months, most babies sit without support, and many can get into a sitting position on their own from lying down. Hands are getting busier too. Watch for your baby moving a toy smoothly from one hand to the other and using a raking motion, all fingers sweeping together, to pull small pieces of food toward themselves. The neat thumb-and-finger pincer grasp typically develops between 9 and 12 months, so messy raking is expected right now. Give plenty of supervised floor time on a firm, safe surface. Sitting, reaching, pivoting, and wobbling are all strength training for the bigger movements coming over the next few months.

Here is the reassurance many parents need: crawling is not on the CDC's nine month milestone checklist. Many healthy babies are not crawling yet at this age, and some scoot on their bottom, roll everywhere, or skip crawling entirely and move straight toward pulling up and walking. What matters more at nine months is steady sitting, active reaching, and a baby who is clearly working on some way to get around. Crawling ages and styles vary so widely that they deserve their own full guide. If your baby seems floppy or stiff, uses one side of the body much more than the other, or is not sitting with support, bring it up with your pediatrician.

Feeding and sleep at nine months

A typical nine month old is settling into roughly three meals a day plus breast milk or formula, which remains an important part of nutrition until the first birthday. Finger foods take center stage now that raking and hand-to-mouth skills are working: soft, cooked pieces about the size of your finger that squash easily when pressed. Many families also start practicing sips of water from an open cup or straw cup at meals. Appetite varies day to day, and that is normal. Your job is to offer a range of safe foods on a steady rhythm; your baby's job is to decide how much to eat.

Most babies this age sleep somewhere between 12 and 16 hours in every 24, including naps, and two naps a day is the typical pattern at nine months. Do not be surprised if sleep gets bumpy for a stretch. New motor skills, separation awareness, and teething can all disturb nights that were previously settled, and these phases usually pass within a few weeks. A short, predictable bedtime routine helps more than any product: feed, wash, pajamas, a book, a song, into the crib awake if you can. Keep the crib bare, put your baby down on their back, and skip pillows, blankets, and bumpers for now.

The nine month checkup and when to call

The nine month well visit is more than a weigh-in. It is one of the ages when the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends formal developmental screening, so expect a written questionnaire about how your baby moves, communicates, plays, and solves small problems. Answer it honestly rather than generously; it works best as a snapshot of a typical day. The visit usually also covers growth measurements, a physical exam, feeding and sleep questions, and safety topics like babyproofing for a baby who is about to be mobile. Jot down questions beforehand, and note dates and answers in the BeMama app or a notebook so nothing gets lost between visits.

Between visits, trust the pattern more than any single day. Talk with your pediatrician if, by nine months, your baby does not sit even with support, does not babble, does not respond to their own name, does not seem to recognize familiar people, or does not bear weight on their legs when you hold them upright. The clearest reason to call at any age is lost skills: a baby who used to babble or sit and has stopped. None of these signs is a diagnosis. They are simply the agreed points where an early check is worthwhile, and when extra support is needed, starting it sooner helps more. When in doubt, ask; that is what the visit is for.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC milestones describe skills that most children can do by a particular age across social, language, thinking, and movement domains. They support observation and conversation but do not replace standardized developmental screening.

Individual skills vary, but caregiver concern matters. Missing several expected skills, losing a skill, or a difference in movement, communication, hearing, or vision should be discussed promptly.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to preserve dated observations, growth, activities, and questions for well-child visits. It cannot label development as normal or delayed.

When to seek help

Contact your child’s healthcare professional whenever you are concerned or notice loss of a skill. Seek urgent care for an acute change, breathing difficulty, loss of responsiveness, or seizure-like activity.

Key takeaways

  • Most 9 month olds sit without support, respond to their name, and babble strings of sounds like mamamama.
  • Stranger shyness, separation protest, and a love of peekaboo are healthy signs of memory and attachment.
  • Crawling is not on the 9 month checklist, and many healthy babies are not crawling yet.
  • The 9 month well visit includes a formal developmental screening questionnaire, so expect detailed questions.
  • Call your pediatrician about not sitting with support, no babbling, no response to their name, or lost skills.

Frequently asked questions

What should a 9 month old be doing?

Most 9 month olds sit without support, move objects from hand to hand, babble strings of sounds, respond to their name, look for objects that fall out of sight, and smile at games like peekaboo. Babies develop on their own timelines, so one skill arriving a little late rarely means a problem on its own. The pattern across weeks matters more than any single day. Your pediatrician screens all of these areas at the 9 month visit.

When do babies respond to their name?

Most babies respond to their name by around 9 months, and many begin turning toward it between 6 and 9 months. The response may look like turning, pausing, or glancing up rather than anything dramatic. Try it in a quiet room, since a busy environment makes any baby harder to reach. If your baby does not respond to their name by 9 months, mention it to your pediatrician.

Is it normal if my 9 month old is not crawling?

Yes. Crawling is not on the CDC's 9 month milestone checklist, and many healthy babies are not crawling at this age. Some scoot, roll, or skip crawling entirely and move straight to pulling up and walking. Talk with your pediatrician if your baby is not sitting with support, seems unusually stiff or floppy, or strongly favors one side of the body.

What happens at the 9 month checkup?

The 9 month checkup includes growth measurements, a physical exam, and a formal developmental screening questionnaire, since 9 months is one of the American Academy of Pediatrics screening ages. Your pediatrician will ask about feeding, sleep, and safety, and may talk through babyproofing before your baby is fully mobile. Vaccines depend on your baby's record: many babies have none due at 9 months, though a third hepatitis B dose, a seasonal flu vaccine, or catch-up doses may be given. It is a good time to bring your own questions.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
